name: Epictetus
worldviewSummary: Epictetus teaches that freedom and happiness depend on distinguishing what is up to us — our judgements, intentions, desires and aversions — from what is not, such as our bodies, reputation and possessions. Suffering arises from our judgements about events, not from events themselves.
biography: Born into slavery in Hierapolis (Phrygia), later freed; taught Stoic philosophy in Rome and, after the expulsion of philosophers, in Nicopolis. He wrote nothing himself; his student Arrian recorded his teaching in the Discourses and the Handbook (Enchiridion). Birth and death years are approximate.

concepts.description: Some things are up to us (judgement, impulse, desire, aversion) and some are not (body, property, reputation, office); peace comes from focusing on the former.
People are disturbed not by things but by their judgements about things.
The rational faculty of choice is the only thing truly ours and cannot be compelled by anyone else.

positions.statement: Freedom is not obtained by satisfying desires but by removing desire for what is not up to us; a person enslaved in body can be free in will.
Of anything you love, remind yourself what kind of thing it is, so that losing it does not overthrow you; never say 'I have lost it' but 'I have given it back'.
Seeking the approval of others makes one dependent on what is not up to us; one should be content to appear foolish in externals for the sake of progress.
We each have roles — as human beings, citizens, children, parents — and our duties are discovered by reflecting on these relationships.

relations.note: Epictetus repeatedly criticized Epicurean ethics in the Discourses.
